items.body:
## Description

When a `Dataset` that contains non-ASCII text (accents, Greek, CJK, ...) is
exported to DBF, the values after that text are written at the wrong byte
offsets. Re-importing the file gives values with extra leading spaces, text
moved into the next column, truncated values, or a `ValueError` when a numeric
field is affected.

Tested on current `master` (b6a75dc), Python 3.15.

## Steps to reproduce

```python
import tablib

data = tablib.Dataset(headers=['word', 'city', 'k'])
data.append(('Ελλάδα', 'Αθήνα', 'x'))
data.append(('España', 'Madrid', 'y'))

for row in tablib.Dataset().load(data.export('dbf'), 'dbf'):
    print(row)
```

Actual:

```
('Ελλάδα', '      Αθήνα', '           x')
('España', ' Madrid', ' y')
```

Expected:

```
('Ελλάδα', 'Αθήνα', 'x')
('España', 'Madrid', 'y')
```

With a long value, text spills into the next column and the original value
there is lost:

```python
data = tablib.Dataset(('é' * 79 + 'x', 'tail'), headers=['a', 'b'])
print(tablib.Dataset().load(data.export('dbf'), 'dbf')[0])
# ('éééé…é' (40 chars), 'éééé…éxt')   <- 'tail' is gone
```

When a numeric column follows, the import fails:

```python
data = tablib.Dataset(headers=['word', 'city', 'n'])
data.append(('é' * 79 + 'x', 'tail', 3))
tablib.Dataset().load(data.export('dbf'), 'dbf')
# ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: b'ail'
```

## Cause

DBF character fields have a fixed width in **bytes** (80 for the fields that
tablib creates). In the vendored dbfpy, `DbfCharacterFieldDef.encodeValue()`
truncates and pads the value by **character** count
(`str(value)[:self.length].ljust(self.length)`), and `DbfRecord._write()` then
encodes the whole record. Each multi-byte character makes the field longer
than its declared width, which moves every following field in the record.
Reading uses the declared offsets and decodes as UTF-8, so the values come back
shifted.
items.title: DBF export corrupts records containing non-ASCII text

items.body:
XLS boolean cells are returned as integer 0 and 1 instead of Python booleans. This changes downstream JSON from false and true to numbers, unlike XLSX imports.

```python
import tablib
source = tablib.Dataset((True, False, 1, 0), headers=['yes', 'no', 'one', 'zero'])
result = tablib.Dataset().load(source.xls, 'xls')
print(result[0])
print(result.json)
```

Current result is `(1, 0, 1.0, 0.0)` and JSON contains 1 and 0 for the first two cells. The expected first two values are `True` and `False`, while the numeric cells should remain numeric. The same issue occurs when importing a Databook.

Reproduced on current master with CPython 3.14.6, xlrd 2.0.2 and xlwt 1.3.0. `XLSFormat.read_cell` converts error and date cells but leaves `XL_CELL_BOOLEAN` values unchanged.
items.title: XLS imports turn boolean cells into numeric values

items.body:
## Description

Dataset.sort() returns the rows in the correct order, but their tags
are lost. Filtering the sorted dataset by an existing tag then returns
no matches, even though the matching row is still present.

## Environment

- Python: 3.13.9
- Operating system: macOS-26.6.2-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O
- Tablib: 3.11.1.dev1+gb6a75dcbe
- Source commit: b6a75dcbe01cc42b3fd45ae5005901e2639fa7a7

## Reproduction

```python
import tablib

data = tablib.Dataset(headers=["name", "score"])
data.append(["Alice", 20], tags=["selected"])
data.append(["Bob", 10], tags=["other"])

print("Before sorting:", list(data.filter("selected")))

sorted_data = data.sort("score")

print("Sorted rows:", list(sorted_data))
print("After sorting:", list(sorted_data.filter("selected")))
print("Original still tagged:", list(data.filter("selected")))
```

## Actual output

```text
Before sorting: [('Alice', 20)]
Sorted rows: [('Bob', 10), ('Alice', 20)]
After sorting: []
Original still tagged: [('Alice', 20)]
```

## Expected behaviour

Sorting should reorder the rows while preserving their tags.

Filtering the sorted dataset for "selected" should still return:

```text
[('Alice', 20)]
```

## Impact

A workflow that tags records, sorts them, and then filters by tag can
silently return an empty result despite the matching records still
being present.

## Possible cause

Dataset.sort() reconstructs rows from their exported values and adds
them to a new Dataset without passing the original row tags.

## Related reports

Issues #51 and #251 discuss filtering by multiple tags. This example
uses a single tag that works before sorting.

PR #704 addresses sorting with duplicate headers. This reproduction
uses unique headers and concerns preservation of row tags.

## Disclosure

I used AI assistance to investigate and prepare this report.
I reproduced the behaviour locally before submitting.
items.title: Dataset.sort() drops row tags, causing subsequent filtering to return no matches

items.body:
Exporting a Dataset with repeated headers to a pandas DataFrame silently replaces distinct column values with the last column sharing that header. This also discards formatters applied to the earlier column.

```python
import tablib

data = tablib.Dataset([1, 2], headers=['value', 'value'])
print(data.export('df').values.tolist())
# Actual [[2, 2]]
# Expected [[1, 2]]
```

Reproduced on current master with Python 3.14 and pandas. DataFrame supports duplicate column labels, so both positional values should survive. The export currently goes through dictionaries, which collapse the repeated keys before pandas receives them.

Upstream commit b6a75dcbe01cc42b3fd45ae5005901e2639fa7a7.
items.title: DataFrame exports overwrite cells when headers repeat

items.body:
ODS datetime exports drop microseconds, and importing an ODS date cell with fractional seconds raises `ValueError` because the parser only accepts whole seconds.

```python
from datetime import datetime
import tablib

value = datetime(2019, 10, 4, 12, 30, 8, 123456)
dataset = tablib.Dataset((value,), headers=["datetime"])
restored = tablib.Dataset().load(dataset.ods, "ods")
print(restored[0][0])
```

This prints `2019-10-04 12:30:08` and loses `123456` microseconds. The round trip should preserve the original datetime.

An externally created date cell with `office:date-value="2019-10-04T12:30:08.123456"` instead raises `ValueError` with `unconverted data remains` on import.

Reproduced on Linux with Python 3.14.6, odfpy 1.4.1 and current master.
items.title: ODS datetime imports reject fractional seconds and exports drop them

items.body:
ODS `Databook` exports reference date and time styles that are missing from the document. `Dataset` exports register these styles, but `export_book()` only registers the bold header style.

```python
import datetime
from io import BytesIO

import tablib
from odf import opendocument, table

dataset = tablib.Dataset(
    (datetime.date(2026, 11, 11), datetime.time(12, 30)),
    headers=("date", "time"),
)
workbook = opendocument.load(BytesIO(tablib.Databook([dataset]).ods))
cells = workbook.spreadsheet.getElementsByType(table.TableRow)[1].childNodes
print([cell.getAttribute("stylename") for cell in cells])
print([node.getAttribute("name") for node in workbook.automaticstyles.childNodes])
```

The cells reference `ds1` and `ts1`, but only `bold` is defined. The corresponding number styles are also absent. These references need to resolve for spreadsheet viewers to apply the intended date and time formats. Reproduced on current master with Python 3.14.6 and odfpy.
items.title: ODS Databook exports omit date and time styles

items.body:
An ODS float cell can store a numeric office:value and show formatted text. Importing a percentage or grouped number raises ValueError. Rounded display text also loses precision. The reader should use the stored numeric value, as it already does for numeric cells without display text.

Reproduced on Python 3.14.6 at b6a75dcb.

```python
from io import BytesIO
import tablib
from odf import opendocument,table,text
doc=opendocument.OpenDocumentSpreadsheet()
sheet=table.Table(name="Data");doc.spreadsheet.addElement(sheet)
row=table.TableRow();sheet.addElement(row)
cell=table.TableCell(valuetype="float",value="0.125");cell.addElement(text.P(text="12.5%"));row.addElement(cell)
stream=BytesIO();doc.save(stream)
dataset=tablib.Dataset().load(BytesIO(stream.getvalue()),format="ods",headers=False)
assert list(dataset)==[(0.125,)]
```

items.body:
## Description

Replacing an existing row in a Dataset containing a dynamic column
accepts only the non-dynamic values, but does not generate the missing
calculated cell.

The row becomes shorter than its headers. JSON export silently omits
the calculated column, and accessing that column raises IndexError.

## Tested source commit

b6a75dcbe01cc42b3fd45ae5005901e2639fa7a7

## Minimal reproduction

```python
import tablib

data = tablib.Dataset(["Alice", 10], headers=["name", "score"])
data.append_col(lambda row: row[1] * 2, header="double")

data[0] = ["Bob", 20]

print(data.headers)
print(data[0])
print(data.json)
print(data["double"])
```

## Actual result

```text
['name', 'score', 'double']
('Bob', 20)
[{"name": "Bob", "score": 20}]
IndexError: list index out of range
```

## Expected result

Replacement should preserve consistent dataset dimensions.

It could generate the missing dynamic value, producing ("Bob", 20, 40),
as append() does. If this form of replacement is unsupported, it should
raise InvalidDimensions before modifying the existing row.

## Control

Using append(["Bob", 20]) on a fresh dataset with the same dynamic
column correctly produces ("Bob", 20, 40).

## Related issue

I found #576 and PR #671. Those concern appending rows containing
callable placeholders.

This reproduction replaces an existing row using Dataset.__setitem__
and supplies only non-dynamic values.

## Environment and actual terminal output

PS C:\Users\Lenovo\Desktop\tablib-bug-report> notepad reproduce.py
PS C:\Users\Lenovo\Desktop\tablib-bug-report> .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe reproduce.py | Tee-Object -FilePath bug-output.txt
Python: 3.13.11
Platform: Windows-11-10.0.26300-SP0
Source commit: b6a75dcbe01cc42b3fd45ae5005901e2639fa7a7
Append control: ('Bob', 20, 40)
Headers: ['name', 'score', 'double']
Replacement row: ('Bob', 20)
JSON: [{"name": "Bob", "score": 20}]
Error: IndexError list index out of range

## Disclosure

I used AI assistance to investigate and prepare this report, and
reproduced the behaviour locally before submitting.
items.title: Row replacement accepts omitted dynamic values and leaves inconsistent dimensions

items.body:
## Description

The reStructuredText exporter writes cell and header content verbatim into the grid table, but in a grid table a `|` ends the cell — so a literal pipe in the data breaks the table structure, and a literal backslash is consumed by reStructuredText as an escape character instead of rendering:

```python
import tablib

data = tablib.Dataset()
data.headers = ['name', 'note']
data.append(['a|b', 'w'])
print(data.export('rst', force_grid=True))
```

outputs

```
+------+------+
| name | note |
+======+======+
| a|b  | w    |       <- 'a|b' contains an unescaped pipe that ends the cell
+------+------+
```

which reStructuredText parses as a cell containing only `a`, leaving the rest as invalid markup. The same happens for headers, and `tablib.Databook.rst` (which always forces the grid format) is affected too.

## Expected behavior

Pipes and backslashes are escaped (`\|`, `\\`), the escape sequences reStructuredText defines, so cells render their content — and the column widths account for the added escape characters so the grid stays aligned.
items.title: reStructuredText export does not escape pipes and backslashes in grid tables

items.body:
## Description

The Jira exporter does not escape pipe characters in cell or header content, although `|` is the cell delimiter in Jira wiki markup — so a literal pipe in the data silently splits the cell:

```python
import tablib

data = tablib.Dataset()
data.headers = ['h | 1', 'plain']
data.append(['a | b', 'x'])
print(data.jira)
```

outputs

```
||h | 1||plain||
|a | b|x|
```

which renders in Jira as a 3-column header (`h`, `1`, `plain`) and a 3-column row instead of the intended 2 columns.

Jira wiki markup escapes a literal pipe with a backslash (`\|`), so cells can keep their pipe content.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a dataset whose header or cell values contain `|`
2. `print(dataset.jira)`
3. The pipe starts a new cell in the rendered table

## Expected behavior

Pipes in header/cell values are escaped as `\|` so they render as content, the same way the LaTeX exporter already escapes TeX reserved symbols.
items.title: Jira export does not escape pipes in cells and headers

items.body:
Found while reviewing table export paths for document conversion. A dataset can have repeated headers, but reStructuredText export routes its rows through dictionaries. The later cell replaces the earlier one and the remaining values no longer line up with the header columns.

Reproduced on current master with Python 3.12.

```python
import tablib

data = tablib.Dataset(["first", "second"], headers=["same", "same"])
print(data.export("rst"))
print(data.export("rst", force_grid=True))
```

Both output table styles omit `first`. Expected both cells under their original column positions, including any column-specific formatters.

The pending RST optimization in #670 explicitly preserves this dictionary behavior rather than fixing it.
items.title: reStructuredText export drops cells when headers repeat

items.body:
### Reproduction

```python
import tablib

data = tablib.Dataset(["unused", 2], headers=["drop", "units"])
data.append_col(lambda row: 99, header="total")
data.append_col([5], header="tail")
del data["drop"]
data.append([3, 7])
print(data.export("csv"))
```

### Expected

```csv
units,total,tail
2,99,5
3,99,7
```

### Actual

```csv
units,total,tail
2,99,5
3,7,99
```

Only the newly appended row is misaligned. A static column after the generated column makes the incorrect position visible; if the dynamic column is last, list insertion can hide the stale index by appending to the end.

Reproduced on Python 3.12 / Linux with Tablib 3.10.0, both the published wheel and master at `b6a75dc`.

items.body:
## Summary

Since tablib 3.10.0, `tablib/__init__.py` declares `__lazy_modules__ = {"tablib.core"}` (#645). On Python 3.15 this means `import tablib` no longer executes `tablib/core.py`, and therefore never runs `registry.register_builtins()` (the call at the bottom of `core.py`).

As a result, `tablib.formats.registry` is empty after `import tablib` until some code happens to touch `tablib.core` (for example by referencing `tablib.Dataset`). Any consumer that resolves formats through the registry directly gets `UnsupportedFormat` for every builtin format, including `csv` and `json`.

On Python 3.14 and earlier the `__lazy_modules__` declaration is ignored, so the registry is populated eagerly as before.

## Reproduction

```python
import tablib
from tablib.formats import registry

print(list(registry._formats))
registry.get_format("csv")
```

Python 3.14.3, tablib 3.10.0:

```
['json', 'csv', 'tsv', 'dbf', 'html', 'jira', 'latex', 'rst', 'sql']
```

Python 3.15.0, tablib 3.10.0:

```
[]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
tablib.exceptions.UnsupportedFormat: Tablib has no format 'csv' or it is not registered.
```

Touching `tablib.core` first (e.g. `import tablib.core`) populates the registry and the lookup succeeds.

## Why it matters

The registry has been populated as a side effect of `import tablib` since the registry was introduced, and `Dataset` relies on the same mechanism. Downstream libraries that call `registry.get_format()` or iterate `registry.formats()` without first instantiating a `Dataset` now see an order-dependent failure that only appears on the newest Python.

A concrete example: django-import-export checks format availability via `registry.get_format()` at startup, and on 3.15 it silently dropped CSV from its default formats because CSV was the first format checked against the empty registry (django-import-export/django-import-export#2210, fixed downstream in django-import-export/django-import-export#2211 by importing `tablib.core` eagerly).

## Suggested fix

Either of these keeps the startup-time benefit for everything except the registration step:

1. Remove `"tablib.core"` from `__lazy_modules__` in `tablib/__init__.py`, so `core` (and hence `register_builtins()`) is imported eagerly as before. The expensive optional format modules are already loaded lazily by the registry's string-path descriptors, so this should cost little.
2. Move the `registry.register_builtins()` call out of `core.py` into `tablib/__init__.py` (or into `tablib/formats/__init__.py`) so registration does not depend on `core` being imported.

Happy to send a PR for whichever approach you prefer.

## Environment

- tablib 3.10.0
- Python 3.15.0 (fails) and 3.14.3 (works)
- macOS, but the behaviour is import-order based and should be platform independent
items.title: Lazy `tablib.core` import leaves `tablib.formats.registry` empty on Python 3.15

items.body:
I noticed the DBF code does the same work over and over.

On import, it reads the whole row again for each field. So a row with 100 fields gets read and decoded 100 times, even though we only need to read it once. It also searches the field names for every value.

On export, it searches the field names again for every cell, even though their positions stay the same.

Could we find the positions once and reuse them? For import, we could also read each row once and take all its values from that row.

The repeated cell work is roughly O(rows × columns²). This could bring that part down to expected O(columns + rows × columns), using O(columns) extra space for the positions. That only describes the repeated cell work; there is still other work, like building the DBF header or writing the file.

Duplicate names, names with different letter cases, bad or empty input, and custom streams/datasets should still work the same as before. Small inputs can keep the old code if the new setup does not help.

The code is in [src/tablib/formats/_dbf.py](https://github.com/jazzband/tablib/blob/966876c76a6378557c1951badc1665b4d1375875/src/tablib/formats/_dbf.py), in DBFFormat.import_set and DBFFormat.export_set.
items.title: Optimize DBF field lookups

items.body:
`Dataset.stack_cols()` joins two datasets side by side. Right now, it looks up each named column again while building the result. On a wide table, that means repeatedly searching the same header lists and building temporary columns.

Could we find each column's position once, then build the output rows directly? For ordinary datasets, that would remove the roughly quadratic header-lookup work. Duplicate headers must still select their first matching column, as they do now; headerless datasets and existing errors should behave the same too.
items.title: Optimize Dataset.stack_cols() lookups

items.body:
Dataset.filter() rebuilds the same requested-tag set for every row, even though the selection hasn't changed.

For example, filtering 10,000 contacts using 100 audience tags rebuilds that same set 10,000 times.

Could we build it once and reuse it? Small inputs could keep the original approach, since the extra checks also take time.

This should only improve performance. Row order, duplicate-tag handling, metadata, generators and existing errors should stay the same.
items.title: Optimize Dataset filter tag lookups

items.body:
`Dataset.subset()` becomes slow on larger datasets because it repeatedly looks up the same column positions for every row. It also searches a list each time it checks whether a row was selected.

These repeated searches are unnecessary. We can calculate the column positions once and store the selected row numbers in a set for faster lookup.

This reduces the time complexity from approximately O(n³) to O(n²) while keeping the existing behavior unchanged.
items.title: Optimize Dataset.subset() to avoid repeated lookups
